examples.label: Broad turn-off, wearer still preferred it

lessons.prompt: Compare how much of the diamond changes at once. Do the centre and outer steps keep taking turns?
lessons.summary: Watch a full rotation. Bright flashes switching between different facets can feel lively; a large group of steps going dark together can leave the stone looking quiet.
lessons.title: Do the steps take turns flashing?

examples.comment: Karl_K liked the movement and face-up design (#51). This is not a measured centre-by-centre benchmark.
examples.label: More active reference

examples.comment: Ibrakeforpossums specifically noticed a relatively static middle in the 2.54ct candidate (#40).
examples.label: Quiet centre

examples.comment: Ibrakeforpossums found the first 2.00ct stone comparatively quiet in the centre (#2).
examples.label: First of two — quieter centre

examples.comment: Ibrakeforpossums and the buyer preferred the second stone's movement (#2–#3), without claiming a universal cut grade.
examples.label: Second of two — comparatively livelier

examples.comment: Karl_K called its dark centre a question for ASET (#9); later buyer video showed a face-up versus tilt tradeoff (#59).
examples.label: Promising, but dark when static

lessons.prompt: Watch the central steps during rotation. Is there changing light return or an area that rarely participates?
lessons.summary: Look under the table, not just around the bright outer edge. A relatively static middle may matter even when the outer steps are busy.
lessons.title: Does the middle stay awake?

examples.label: Leakage concern

examples.comment: 0-0-0 cautioned that reflections of the surroundings can resemble tilt windowing in the purchased stone (#54).
examples.label: Reflection may mimic leakage

examples.comment: Karl_K localized apparent face-up leakage to the top/bottom central V regions between windmills (#9), rather than judging all dark pixels alike.
examples.label: Specific P3 leakage concern

lessons.prompt: Can the weak-looking steps flash on and off as you move? Does stronger tilt reveal a view through the stone?
lessons.summary: Tilt the stone slowly. Some grey or dark regions are reflections or temporary contrast; persistently transparent under-table steps can instead signal light leakage.
lessons.title: Does an area flash, or stay see-through?

examples.comment: 0-0-0 saw more face-up obstruction than preferred, but acknowledged different tastes for contrast (#17).
examples.label: Stronger obstruction

examples.comment: 0-0-0 preferred its cut; lovedogs worried about darkness at some angles; Karl_K saw potential (#20–#28).
examples.label: Promising, with reservations

examples.comment: Karl_K found the very small windmills less satisfactory even though the stone was not uniformly poor (#9).
examples.label: Tiny windmills — cut feels off

examples.comment: Karl_K saw a Royal-Asscher-like facet arrangement but much weaker light performance (#12).
examples.label: Facet architecture is not enough

examples.comment: The thread author—not Karl_K—identified adjacent dark facets and messy arrow organization (#1).
examples.label: Disorganized black facets

examples.comment: Experienced members liked the small table, outline and balanced contrast (#30–#45), though grade labels conflict.
examples.label: Positive small-table example

lessons.prompt: Compare the face-up pattern, then rotate. Does contrast alternate into bright flashes—or linger across too much of the stone?
lessons.summary: Dark facets are not automatically bad. Controlled contrast can give step cuts depth and structure, while excessive face-up obstruction or prolonged darkness may overwhelm the pattern.
lessons.title: Is the darkness useful contrast?

annotated_source.label: View purchaser's original ASET/photo album; see expert reassessment #20–#23

examples.label: Judgement reversed after ASET

examples.comment: Karl_K wanted ASET before committing (#9); the later owner found the static centre dark but enjoyed the tilted flashes (#59).
examples.label: Vendor spin and real-life tradeoff

examples.comment: Inked preferred the G (#14); Karl_K tentatively favoured the H on limited video, without rejecting the G (#17).
examples.label: Limited comparison is not a verdict

lessons.prompt: Which evidence did each reviewer see, and which questions remained unresolved?
lessons.summary: A promising vendor spin may not tell the full story. Compare the original expectation with later photographs, ASET and the buyer's experience; expert opinions can reasonably change.
lessons.title: What changes after ASET or home viewing?

examples.comment: Karl_K explicitly identified leakage in the top/bottom central V between windmills (#9), also noting a low crown (#10).
examples.label: Crispest: top/bottom P3 region

examples.comment: 0-0-0 described non-flashing central steps and through-view on stronger tilt (#29/#32).
examples.label: Under-table steps that fail to flash

lessons.prompt: Compare the V-shaped steps between the windmills and how those steps change as the stone moves.
lessons.summary: Experienced reviewers sometimes point to precise step regions rather than a general dark impression. The same grey-looking area might be leakage, contrast or a video-lighting effect.
lessons.title: Can you identify which steps fail to return light?

examples.comment: Ibrakeforpossums observed quieter movement in the first stone (#2), supported by the shared side-by-side source video.
examples.label: First: quieter central steps

examples.comment: Ibrakeforpossums and the buyer preferred the second (#2–#3); the buyer later reported it had sold (#5).
examples.label: Second: preferred motion

lessons.prompt: Watch the first and second 2.00ct E VVS2 stones side by side. Which centre changes more often? Neither proportions nor price alone settle the question.
lessons.summary: Carat, colour and clarity are labels, not direct measurements of how an Asscher dances. Comparing two same-spec stones makes the changing central steps easier to notice.
lessons.title: Can two almost identical stones look different?

annotated_source.label: Buyer in-hand comparison and final ring reports (#66–#72)

examples.comment: Experienced members preferred its table, octagonal outline and active contrast (#30–#45); forum grade claims conflict.
examples.label: Smaller contender: community favourite

examples.comment: lovedogs objected to broad darkening (#55), but Dreamer_D liked its spread and corners (#68), and the wearer chose it (#71).
examples.label: Larger contender: eventual wearer choice

examples.comment: lovedogs and Ibrakeforpossums preferred the 3.03ct in the buyer's side-by-side comparison (#66–#69).
examples.label: Home comparison: different preferred cut

lessons.prompt: Contrast expert criticism with the buyer's later side-by-side videos and eventual choice. Which trade-offs matter to you?
lessons.summary: Reviewers can disagree about contrast, windmill size and apparent spread. A buyer may reasonably choose a different stone after seeing both in real life.
lessons.title: Does the technically favoured diamond always win?
